Here are practical, evidence-based tips drawn from our earlier conversations that should help keep your kitchen tidy and manageable:

1. Daily habits
- Wipe countertops after cooking so crumbs and spills don’t build up. Let things cool, then transfer food scraps into the trash (or compost) rather than leaving them in the sink.
- Put utensils back in their assigned spot after use to avoid countertop clutter.

2. Utensil organization
- Purge duplicates and group similar items (spoons, spatulas, whisks).
- Assign each group a specific spot in your new utensil holder so returning items becomes a habit — this keeps counters clutter-free.

3. Garbage disposal maintenance
- Clean periodically: pour 1/2 cup baking soda down the drain followed by 1 cup vinegar, let sit 1–2 hours, then rinse with hot water.
- For stuck debris or odors, run a few ice cubes with rock salt through the disposal to help dislodge and clean the blades.

4. Faucet leaks
- Inspect the faucet to find the leak source (aerator, spout, base). Turn off the supply, check aerator, O-rings, gaskets, and valve seats for wear.
- Replace small worn parts (O-rings, aerator) if that’s the problem; consider a full replacement only if multiple components are failing or repairs don’t stop the leak.

5. Granite countertop scratches
- Assess scratch depth: shallow scratches can sometimes be improved with DIY methods; deep scratches may need a professional.
- For minor surface scratches, cleaning and careful polishing/repair kits can help; for longer or deeper ones, seek a specialist.

6. Storage and leftover care
- Cool hot foods/sauces to near room temperature before refrigerating to avoid bacterial growth.
- Store in airtight containers; many sauces (like Alfredo) keep 3–5 days in the fridge and can be reheated gently.

If you want, I can turn these into a simple daily/weekly checklist or help prioritize which repairs (faucet, disposal, countertop) to tackle first based on effort and cost.

Have fun at the store — here are focused things to try and compare based on what you’ve already asked about (Les Paul, Strat, open tunings, coil‑splits, etc.):

- Try different body/neck constructions and feel: compare a Strat-style (bolt-on, contoured) and a Les Paul-style (set neck, single-cut) to see which neck profile and body weight suit you.
- Listen for pickup types: single‑coils vs humbuckers. Humbuckers (Les Paul) tend to sound warmer, thicker, and sustain more; single‑coils (Strat) are brighter and snappier. If a humbucker feels too thick for some parts of your playing, try a guitar with coil‑splitting/coil‑tap to get more tonal options.
- Test how it responds to tunings you use: if you play open D (or other alternate tunings), try the guitar in that tuning or simulate lower tension — heavier string gauges were recommended for open D to keep a full tone, so check how different gauges feel.
- Play for set‑up and playability: check action, fret access, neck comfort, and intonation up the neck. A well‑setup instrument will make alternate tunings and fingerpicking easier.
